before: The typical symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx [1].

Pathogenic factors include abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, and anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia [2].
GERD is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs), and symptoms potentially attributable to GERD are among the most commonly reported in outpatient primary care [1] [3].
Long-term PPI use is associated with bone fractures, chronic and acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection [1].
A MedGen record is titled Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) [4], and a literature entity is named Gastroesophageal Reflux [5].
